claim: ~80% of cardiac macrophages in 12-week-old Tnfsf11aCre;Rosa26fs-eYFP mice are derived from yolk sac erythro-myeloid progenitors (EMPs).
source: ~80% of cardiac macrophages expressed YFP in hearts of 12-week-old animals, whereas blood monocytes were not labeled (Figure 2A; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data showing YFP expression in cardiac macrophages from Tnfsf11aCre;Rosa26fs-eYFP mice, with quantification shown in Figure 2A.

claim: ~20% of cardiac macrophages are derived from definitive hematopoietic stem cells (HSC).
source: In a comparative analysis, we traced fetal and adult definitive hematopoiesis in Flt3CreRosa26fs-eYFP mice (Gomez Perdiguero et al., 2015; Schulz et al., 2012), indicating that ~20% of cardiac macrophages derived from definitive HSC (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by lineage tracing data in Flt3CreRosa26fs-eYFP mice showing YFP expression in cardiac macrophages, with quantification in Figure 2B.

claim: The majority of resident macrophages in the healthy heart is of early embryonic origin.
source: Thus, the majority of resident macrophages in the healthy heart is of early embryonic origin.
evidence: Inferred from the combined lineage tracing data showing ~80% EMP-derived and ~20% HSC-derived cardiac macrophages.

claim: Cardiac macrophages are reduced by ~90% in Csf1r∆FIRE/∆FIRE mice.
source: We first confirmed that cardiac macrophages in Csf1r∆FIRE/∆FIRE mice (further termed ∆FIRE) mice were reduced by ~90% and the number of monocytes and neutrophils was not altered (Figure 2C–G).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry and histology data showing macrophage quantification in control and ∆FIRE mice, presented in Figure 2C-G.

claim: The number of monocytes and neutrophils is not altered in Csf1r∆FIRE/∆FIRE mice.
source: We first confirmed that cardiac macrophages in Csf1r∆FIRE/∆FIRE mice (further termed ∆FIRE) mice were reduced by ~90% and the number of monocytes and neutrophils was not altered (Figure 2C–G).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data showing quantification of neutrophils and Ly6chi monocytes in control and ∆FIRE mice, presented in Figure 2D.

claim: The macrophages absent in ∆FIRE animals are EMP-derived macrophages.
source: We thus crossed the ∆FIRE animals with the YS EMP fate-mapping line (Tnfsf11aCreRosa26fs-eYFP mice) and showed that the macrophages absent in ∆FIRE animals were EMP-derived macrophages (Figure 2E), thus offering a new model to investigate the role of resident macrophages in cardiac injury.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data showing YFP expression in macrophages from Csf1rΔFIRE/+Tnfsf11aCreRosa26fs-eYFP and Csf1rΔFIRE/ΔFIRETnfsf11aCreRosa26fs-eYFP mice, presented in Figure 2E.

claim: Acute depletion of EMP-derived macrophages using diphtheria toxin results in premature death within 24 hours.
source: Administration of a single DT dose, however, resulted in premature death of all mice (n = 6) within 24 hr (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by survival data from Tnfsf11aCreRosa26fs-DTR mice after DT injection, shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Acute depletion of EMP-derived macrophages induces a systemic inflammatory response syndrome-like phenotype.
source: The injected mice presented with a systemic inflammatory response syndrome-like phenotype, indicating that acute depletion of EMP-derived macrophages is not viable.
evidence: Inferred from observations of body temperature and left ventricular diastolic volume changes after DT injection in Tnfsf11aCreRosa26fs-DTR mice, shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2D-E.

claim: Two clusters of macrophages expressing homeostatic genes (e.g. Lyve1, Gas6, Stab1) are specifically ablated in ∆FIRE mice.
source: Two clusters of macrophages expressing homeostatic (e.g. Lyve1, Gas6, Stab1) and antigen presentation-related genes (e.g. Cd74, H2-Ab1) were specifically ablated in ∆FIRE mice (Figure 3C), which largely represent YFP-expressing macrophages in Tnfsf11aCreRosa26fs-eYFP mice (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by single-cell RNA-sequencing data showing cluster abundance differences between control and ∆FIRE mice, presented in Figure 3C.

claim: Two clusters of macrophages expressing antigen presentation-related genes (e.g. Cd74, H2-Ab1) are specifically ablated in ∆FIRE mice.
source: Two clusters of macrophages expressing homeostatic (e.g. Lyve1, Gas6, Stab1) and antigen presentation-related genes (e.g. Cd74, H2-Ab1) were specifically ablated in ∆FIRE mice (Figure 3C), which largely represent YFP-expressing macrophages in Tnfsf11aCreRosa26fs-eYFP mice (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by single-cell RNA-sequencing data showing cluster abundance differences between control and ∆FIRE mice, presented in Figure 3C.

claim: ~90% of yfp transcripts map to the two clusters of homeostatic and antigen-presenting macrophages that are ablated in ∆FIRE.
source: Specifically, we mapped ~90% of yfp transcripts to the two clusters of homeostatic and antigen-presenting macrophages that were ablated in ∆FIRE.
evidence: Supported by single-cell RNA-sequencing analysis of Tnfsf11aCreRosa26fs-eYFP mice showing YFP expression distribution across macrophage clusters, presented in Figure 3D.

claim: Cx3cr1hi macrophages contain 2% YFP+ cells in Tnfsf11aCreRosa26fs-eYFP mice.
source: Other clusters were not reduced in ∆FIRE, and also were not quantitatively represented in the YS macrophage lineage tracing model, that is Cx3cr1hi (2% YFP), Ccr2lowLy6clo (5% YFP), and Ccr2hiLy6chi (1% YFP) macrophages within respective clusters (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by single-cell RNA-sequencing data showing YFP expression in different macrophage clusters, presented in Figure 3D.

claim: Ccr2lowLy6clo macrophages contain 5% YFP+ cells in Tnfsf11aCreRosa26fs-eYFP mice.
source: Other clusters were not reduced in ∆FIRE, and also were not quantitatively represented in the YS macrophage lineage tracing model, that is Cx3cr1hi (2% YFP), Ccr2lowLy6clo (5% YFP), and Ccr2hiLy6chi (1% YFP) macrophages within respective clusters (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by single-cell RNA-sequencing data showing YFP expression in different macrophage clusters, presented in Figure 3D.

claim: Ccr2hiLy6chi macrophages contain 1% YFP+ cells in Tnfsf11aCreRosa26fs-eYFP mice.
source: Other clusters were not reduced in ∆FIRE, and also were not quantitatively represented in the YS macrophage lineage tracing model, that is Cx3cr1hi (2% YFP), Ccr2lowLy6clo (5% YFP), and Ccr2hiLy6chi (1% YFP) macrophages within respective clusters (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by single-cell RNA-sequencing data showing YFP expression in different macrophage clusters, presented in Figure 3D.

claim: No changes in gene expression or cell numbers are observed in Ly6chi monocytes and inflammatory Ccr2hiLy6chi macrophages in ∆FIRE mice.
source: The specific impact of ∆FIRE on resident macrophages is further supported by the observation, that no changes in gene expression nor cell numbers were observed in Ly6chi monocytes and inflammatory Ccr2hiLy6chi macrophages (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by single-cell RNA-sequencing data showing cluster abundance and gene expression in control and ∆FIRE mice, presented in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Absence of resident macrophages in ∆FIRE is associated with changes in gene expression in non-macrophage clusters such as T- and B-cells and natural killer (NK) cells.
source: Absence of resident macrophages in ∆FIRE was associated with changes in gene expression in non-macrophage clusters such as T- and B-cells and natural killer (NK) cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by single-cell RNA-sequencing data showing differential gene expression in non-macrophage immune cell clusters, presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: Overall phagocytic capacity is reduced in ∆FIRE mice.
source: Furthermore, overall phagocytic capacity, as inferred by expression of phagocytosis-related genes (Amorim et al., 2022), was reduced (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by computed phagocytosis score from single-cell RNA-sequencing data, presented in Figure 3E, based on expression of phagocytosis-related genes.

claim: Left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) improved in control mice from day 6 to day 30 after I/R injury.
source: Function of the cardiac left ventricle (LV), as determined by ejection fraction (LVEF) and stroke volume (SV), improved in controls in the course of post-I/R remodeling (Figure 4B, C).
evidence: Supported by PET imaging data showing LVEF measurements at day 6 and day 30 after I/R injury in control mice, presented in Figure 4B and 4D.

claim: Stroke volume (SV) improved in control mice from day 6 to day 30 after I/R injury.
source: Function of the cardiac left ventricle (LV), as determined by ejection fraction (LVEF) and stroke volume (SV), improved in controls in the course of post-I/R remodeling (Figure 4B, C).
evidence: Supported by PET imaging data showing stroke volume measurements at day 6 and day 30 after I/R injury in control mice, presented in Figure 4C and 4F.

claim: LVEF remained unchanged or worsened in ∆FIRE mice from day 6 to day 30 after I/R injury.
source: In contrast, LVEF and SV remained unchanged or worsened in ∆FIRE mice, and longitudinal observations of mice indicated a negative net effect on ejection fraction from day 6 to 30 post I/R.
evidence: Supported by PET imaging data showing LVEF measurements at day 6 and day 30 after I/R injury in ∆FIRE mice, presented in Figure 4B and 4D.

claim: Absence of resident macrophages negatively influenced cardiac remodeling in the course of infarct healing.
source: Thus, absence of resident macrophages negatively influenced cardiac remodeling in the course of infarct healing (Figure 4D–G).
evidence: Supported by PET imaging data showing cardiac function parameters in control and ∆FIRE mice after I/R injury, presented in Figure 4D-G.

claim: Infarct size as determined by viability defect (PET) was not different between control and ∆FIRE mice after 30 days.
source: Infarct size as determined by viability defect (PET) and fibrotic area (histology) was not different after 30 days (Figure 4E–H).
evidence: Supported by PET imaging data showing viability defect measurements at day 30 after I/R injury, presented in Figure 4E.

claim: Infarct size as determined by fibrotic area (histology) was not different between control and ∆FIRE mice after 30 days.
source: Infarct size as determined by viability defect (PET) and fibrotic area (histology) was not different after 30 days (Figure 4E–H).
evidence: Supported by histological data showing fibrotic area quantification at day 30 after I/R injury, presented in Figure 4H.

claim: Macrophages are largely absent in the remote zone of infarcted hearts in ∆FIRE mice.
source: In ∆FIRE mice, macrophages were largely absent in the remote zone of infarcted hearts (Figure 5A), indicating sustained depletion of resident macrophages.
evidence: Supported by immunohistology data showing macrophage quantification in different cardiac zones 30 days after I/R injury, presented in Figure 5A.

claim: Macrophage numbers in the infarct and border zones are not different between ∆FIRE and control mice after I/R injury.
source: However, macrophages strongly increased in the infarct area and their numbers were not different in both infarct and border zones between ∆FIRE and control mice (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by immunohistology data showing macrophage quantification in infarct and border zones 30 days after I/R injury, presented in Figure 5A.

claim: Bone marrow-derived macrophages are recruited to the infarct area in the early phase of I/R injury.
source: Indeed, complementing lineage tracing of bone marrow (BM) hematopoietic stem cells (HSC) in Flt3Cre mice (Figure 5B) and YS EMP in Tnfsf11aCre mice (Figure 5C) proved the recruitment of macrophages from BM HSC (Flt3 GFP+ and Tnfsf11a RFP−, respectively) in the early phase of I/R injury.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data from Flt3CreRosa26fs-mT/mG and Tnfsf11aCreRosa26RFP mice showing macrophage origin 2 days after I/R injury, presented in Figure 5B and 5C.

claim: BM-derived macrophages represent ~75% of macrophages in the infarct zone 30 days after I/R injury.
source: 30 days after I/R, BM-derived macrophages remained overrepresented in the infarct zone (~75% HSC contribution), and differential contribution of BM HSC declined from the border zone (~50%) to the remote zone (~35%) (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by histological analysis of Flt3CreRosa26fs-mT/mG mice showing GFP+ macrophage quantification in different cardiac zones 30 days after I/R injury, presented in Figure 5D.

claim: BM-derived macrophages represent ~50% of macrophages in the border zone 30 days after I/R injury.
source: 30 days after I/R, BM-derived macrophages remained overrepresented in the infarct zone (~75% HSC contribution), and differential contribution of BM HSC declined from the border zone (~50%) to the remote zone (~35%) (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by histological analysis of Flt3CreRosa26fs-mT/mG mice showing GFP+ macrophage quantification in different cardiac zones 30 days after I/R injury, presented in Figure 5D.

claim: BM-derived macrophages represent ~35% of macrophages in the remote zone 30 days after I/R injury.
source: 30 days after I/R, BM-derived macrophages remained overrepresented in the infarct zone (~75% HSC contribution), and differential contribution of BM HSC declined from the border zone (~50%) to the remote zone (~35%) (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by histological analysis of Flt3CreRosa26fs-mT/mG mice showing GFP+ macrophage quantification in different cardiac zones 30 days after I/R injury, presented in Figure 5D.

claim: Recruited BM-derived macrophages represent the main population in the infarct area after I/R injury.
source: Taken together, recruited BM-derived macrophages represent the main population in the infarct area and their recruitment was unaltered in ∆FIRE mice.
evidence: Inferred from lineage tracing data showing high proportion of BM-derived macrophages in the infarct zone, presented in Figure 5B-D.

claim: Recruitment of BM-derived macrophages is unaltered in ∆FIRE mice.
source: Taken together, recruited BM-derived macrophages represent the main population in the infarct area and their recruitment was unaltered in ∆FIRE mice.
evidence: Supported by immunohistology data showing similar macrophage numbers in infarct and border zones between control and ∆FIRE mice, presented in Figure 5A.

claim: Resident and recruited macrophages exhibit profound transcriptional differences after I/R injury.
source: The two macrophage populations exhibited profound transcriptional differences after I/R injury.
evidence: Supported by bulk RNA sequencing data comparing CD45.1+ (recruited) and CD45.2+ (resident) macrophages 2 days after I/R injury, presented in Figure 6B-D.

claim: Expression of homeostasis-related genes like Timd4, Lyve1, Cd163, and Retnla is increased in resident CD45.2+ macrophages after I/R injury.
source: Expression of homeostasis-related genes like Timd4, Lyve1, Cd163, and Retnla was increased in resident CD45.2+ macrophages (Figure 6B, C).
evidence: Supported by bulk RNA sequencing data showing differential gene expression between CD45.1+ and CD45.2+ macrophages, presented in Figure 6B and 6C.

claim: CD45.1+ recruited macrophages upregulate inflammatory- and host defense-related gene ontology terms after I/R injury.
source: Substantiating the differential regulation of macrophage programs, CD45.1+ macrophages increased inflammatory- and host defense-related gene ontology (GO) terms (e.g. myeloid leukocyte-related immunity, killing of cells), whereas CD45.2+ macrophages upregulated development- and homeostasis-related GO terms (e.g. extracellular matrix organization, vasculature development, heart muscle development) (Figure 6D).
evidence: Supported by gene ontology enrichment analysis of bulk RNA sequencing data from CD45.1+ and CD45.2+ macrophages, presented in Figure 6D.

claim: CD45.2+ resident macrophages upregulate development- and homeostasis-related gene ontology terms after I/R injury.
source: Substantiating the differential regulation of macrophage programs, CD45.1+ macrophages increased inflammatory- and host defense-related gene ontology (GO) terms (e.g. myeloid leukocyte-related immunity, killing of cells), whereas CD45.2+ macrophages upregulated development- and homeostasis-related GO terms (e.g. extracellular matrix organization, vasculature development, heart muscle development) (Figure 6D).
evidence: Supported by gene ontology enrichment analysis of bulk RNA sequencing data from CD45.1+ and CD45.2+ macrophages, presented in Figure 6D.

claim: Processes involved in innate immunity are increased in CD45.1+ recruited macrophages after infarction.
source: GO enrichment analysis further predicted that processes involved in innate (e.g. leukocyte migration, regulation of defense response, response to bacterium) as well as the adaptive immunity (e.g. T cell selection, T cell activation, B cell proliferation) were increased in CD45.1+ macrophages after infarction (Figure 6D).
evidence: Supported by gene ontology enrichment analysis of bulk RNA sequencing data from CD45.1+ macrophages, presented in Figure 6D.

claim: Processes involved in adaptive immunity are increased in CD45.1+ recruited macrophages after infarction.
source: GO enrichment analysis further predicted that processes involved in innate (e.g. leukocyte migration, regulation of defense response, response to bacterium) as well as the adaptive immunity (e.g. T cell selection, T cell activation, B cell proliferation) were increased in CD45.1+ macrophages after infarction (Figure 6D).
evidence: Supported by gene ontology enrichment analysis of bulk RNA sequencing data from CD45.1+ macrophages, presented in Figure 6D.

claim: Abundance of homeostatic macrophages is reduced in ∆FIRE mice 2 days after I/R injury.
source: In contrast to the absence of homeostatic and antigen-presenting macrophage clusters in healthy hearts of ∆FIRE mice (Figure 3B, C), there were less differences in immune cell clusters between ∆FIRE and control mice 2 days after I/R (Figure 7). Abundance of homeostatic macrophages was also reduced at this time point, however, other clusters including Ccr2hiLy6chi inflammatory macrophages were not altered, which is in line with our histological findings.
evidence: Supported by single-cell RNA-sequencing data showing cluster abundance differences between control and ∆FIRE mice 2 days after I/R injury, presented in Figure 7C.

claim: Ccr2hiLy6chi inflammatory macrophages are not altered in ∆FIRE mice 2 days after I/R injury.
source: Abundance of homeostatic macrophages was also reduced at this time point, however, other clusters including Ccr2hiLy6chi inflammatory macrophages were not altered, which is in line with our histological findings.
evidence: Supported by single-cell RNA-sequencing data showing cluster abundance differences between control and ∆FIRE mice 2 days after I/R injury, presented in Figure 7C.

claim: Expression of anti-inflammatory genes like Chil3 and Lcn2 is reduced across different immune cell clusters in ∆FIRE mice after I/R injury.
source: Across different clusters, including lymphocyte and neutrophil clusters, expression of anti-inflammatory genes like Chil3 (Ym1) and Lcn2 was reduced.
evidence: Supported by single-cell RNA-sequencing data showing gene expression in different immune cell clusters, presented in Figure 7—figure supplements 1–3.

claim: Expression of Bcl-family genes like Blc2a1a and Bcl2a1d is higher in ∆FIRE mice after I/R injury.
source: Vice versa, expression of Bcl-family genes like Blc2a1a and Bcl2a1d, which are associated with apoptosis and inflammatory pathways, was higher in ∆FIRE mice (Figure 7—figure supplements 1–3).
evidence: Supported by single-cell RNA-sequencing data showing gene expression in different immune cell clusters, presented in Figure 7—figure supplements 1–3.

claim: Expression of antigen presentation-related genes (e.g. Cd74, H2-Ab1) is upregulated in Ccr2loLy6clo, homeostatic and Ccr2hiLy6chi macrophage clusters in ∆FIRE mice after I/R injury.
source: Other upregulated genes were related to antigen presentation (e.g.Cd74, H2-Ab1), as identified in the Ccr2loLy6clo, homeostatic and Ccr2hiLy6chi macrophage clusters (Figure 7—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: Supported by single-cell RNA-sequencing data showing differential gene expression in macrophage clusters, presented in Figure 7—figure supplements 1 and 2.

claim: Inflammasome activation score is increased in all neutrophil clusters in ∆FIRE mice after I/R injury.
source: Furthermore, we interrogated inflammatory gene expression in neutrophils, which are abundant first responders to myocardial infarction. We found that a computed score summing up inflammasome activation (Amorim et al., 2022) was increased in all neutrophil clusters in ∆FIRE mice (Figure 7D).
evidence: Supported by computed inflammasome score from single-cell RNA-sequencing data, presented in Figure 7D, based on expression of inflammasome-related genes.

claim: The number of ligand-receptor interactions with neutrophils and lymphocytes is markedly reduced in homeostatic, antigen-presenting, and Ccr2loLy6clo macrophage clusters in ∆FIRE mice after I/R injury.
source: Indeed, the number of LR interactions with neutrophils and lymphocytes, as well as the strength of the macrophage-emitted communication signals was markedly reduced in homeostatic, antigen-presenting, and Ccr2loLy6clo macrophage clusters (Figure 7E, F, Figure 7—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Supported by ligand-receptor interaction analysis from single-cell RNA-sequencing data, presented in Figure 7E, F, and Figure 7—figure supplement 4.

claim: The strength of macrophage-emitted communication signals is markedly reduced in homeostatic, antigen-presenting, and Ccr2loLy6clo macrophage clusters in ∆FIRE mice after I/R injury.
source: Indeed, the number of LR interactions with neutrophils and lymphocytes, as well as the strength of the macrophage-emitted communication signals was markedly reduced in homeostatic, antigen-presenting, and Ccr2loLy6clo macrophage clusters (Figure 7E, F, Figure 7—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Supported by ligand-receptor interaction analysis from single-cell RNA-sequencing data, presented in Figure 7E, F, and Figure 7—figure supplement 4.

claim: Immune cell communication in BM-derived macrophage clusters is not different between ∆FIRE and control mice after I/R injury.
source: In contrast, immune cell communication in BM-derived macrophage clusters (e.g. Ccr2hiLy6chi macrophage cluster, Figure 7—figure supplement 5) was not different to control mice.
evidence: Supported by ligand-receptor interaction analysis from single-cell RNA-sequencing data, presented in Figure 7—figure supplement 5.

claim: Transcriptional profiles of BM-derived inflammatory macrophages are largely unaltered in ∆FIRE mice after I/R injury.
source: Taken together, deficiency in resident macrophages in I/R injury altered the intercellular immune crosstalk and induced a proinflammatory signature in for example cardiac neutrophils. However, transcriptional profiles of BM-derived inflammatory macrophages were largely unaltered.
evidence: Supported by single-cell RNA-sequencing data showing gene expression in BM-derived macrophage clusters, presented in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: Continuous treatment with CSF1R-inhibitor PLX5622 results in the absence of cardiac macrophages within 7 days in healthy hearts.
source: In healthy hearts, inhibitor treatment resulted in the absence of cardiac macrophages within 7 days (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data showing macrophage quantification in hearts from mice treated with PLX5622 for 7 days, presented in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: Treatment with PLX5622 diminishes macrophage numbers in both remote and infarct areas 2 days after I/R injury.
source: Treatment with PLX5622 diminished macrophage numbers in both remote and infarct areas in the early phase (day 2) after injury.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data showing macrophage quantification in remote and ischemic myocardium 2 days after I/R injury in PLX5622-treated mice, presented in Figure 8B.

claim: Recruitment of neutrophils is not altered by PLX5622 treatment after I/R injury.
source: Recruitment of other myeloid cells for example neutrophils was not altered in this context (Figure 8B).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data showing neutrophil quantification in remote and ischemic myocardium 2 days after I/R injury in PLX5622-treated mice, presented in Figure 8B.

claim: Macrophages are largely absent in remote, border, and infarct zones 30 days after I/R injury in PLX5622-treated mice.
source: This effect was pronounced in the chronic phase (day 30) after I/R injury, in which macrophages were largely absent in remote, border, and infarct zones (Figure 8C, D).
evidence: Supported by immunohistology data showing macrophage quantification in different cardiac zones 30 days after I/R injury in PLX5622-treated mice, presented in Figure 8C and 8D.

claim: Absence of resident and recruited macrophages is associated with increased infarct size after I/R injury.
source: Absence of resident and recruited macrophages was associated increased infarct size, as determined by fibrosis area (WGA histology) as well as viability defect (PET), and resulted in deterioration of cardiac function (Figure 8E–I).
evidence: Supported by histology and PET imaging data showing infarct size measurements in PLX5622-treated mice after I/R injury, presented in Figure 8F and 8I.

claim: Absence of resident and recruited macrophages results in deterioration of cardiac function after I/R injury.
source: Absence of resident and recruited macrophages was associated increased infarct size, as determined by fibrosis area (WGA histology) as well as viability defect (PET), and resulted in deterioration of cardiac function (Figure 8E–I).
evidence: Supported by PET imaging data showing cardiac function parameters in PLX5622-treated mice after I/R injury, presented in Figure 8E-H.

claim: LVEF is reduced 6 days after I/R injury in PLX5622-treated mice.
source: Specifically, LVEF was reduced 6 days after I/R, and remained strongly impaired at 30 days (Figure 8E).
evidence: Supported by PET imaging data showing LVEF measurements at day 6 and day 30 after I/R injury in PLX5622-treated mice, presented in Figure 8E.

claim: LVEF remains strongly impaired at 30 days after I/R injury in PLX5622-treated mice.
source: Specifically, LVEF was reduced 6 days after I/R, and remained strongly impaired at 30 days (Figure 8E).
evidence: Supported by PET imaging data showing LVEF measurements at day 6 and day 30 after I/R injury in PLX5622-treated mice, presented in Figure 8E.

claim: Sole absence of resident macrophages has limited negative impact on cardiac remodeling after I/R injury.
source: Taken together, sole absence of resident macrophages had limited negative impact on cardiac remodeling.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of cardiac outcomes in ∆FIRE mice (resident macrophage depletion) versus PLX5622-treated mice (both resident and recruited macrophage depletion), presented in Figures 4 and 8.

claim: Absence of both resident and recruited macrophages results in a significant increase in infarct size after I/R injury.
source: Absence of both resident and recruited macrophages resulted in a significant increase in infarct size and deterioration of left ventricular function after I/R injury, highlighting a beneficial effect of recruited macrophages in cardiac healing.
evidence: Supported by histology and PET imaging data showing increased infarct size in PLX5622-treated mice after I/R injury, presented in Figure 8F and 8I.

claim: Absence of both resident and recruited macrophages results in deterioration of left ventricular function after I/R injury.
source: Absence of both resident and recruited macrophages resulted in a significant increase in infarct size and deterioration of left ventricular function after I/R injury, highlighting a beneficial effect of recruited macrophages in cardiac healing.
evidence: Supported by PET imaging data showing cardiac function parameters in PLX5622-treated mice after I/R injury, presented in Figure 8E-H.

claim: Recruited macrophages have a beneficial effect in cardiac healing after I/R injury.
source: Absence of both resident and recruited macrophages resulted in a significant increase in infarct size and deterioration of left ventricular function after I/R injury, highlighting a beneficial effect of recruited macrophages in cardiac healing.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of cardiac outcomes in ∆FIRE mice (resident macrophage depletion) versus PLX5622-treated mice (both resident and recruited macrophage depletion), showing worse outcomes with combined depletion.

claim: Resident macrophages orchestrate inflammatory responses improving cardiac remodeling after I/R injury.
source: In summary, resident macrophages orchestrate inflammatory responses improving cardiac remodeling, while recruited macrophages determine infarct size after I/R injury.
evidence: Inferred from combined data showing altered immune cell crosstalk and adverse remodeling in ∆FIRE mice, presented in Figures 4 and 7.

claim: Recruited macrophages determine infarct size after I/R injury.
source: In summary, resident macrophages orchestrate inflammatory responses improving cardiac remodeling, while recruited macrophages determine infarct size after I/R injury.
evidence: Inferred from data showing increased infarct size when both resident and recruited macrophages are depleted (PLX5622 treatment) but not when only resident macrophages are absent (∆FIRE), presented in Figures 4 and 8.

claim: Macrophages are the most abundant immune cell population in healthy cardiovascular tissues.
source: They represent the most abundant immune cell population in healthy cardiovascular tissues (Heidt et al., 2014; Weinberger et al., 2020), where they contribute to organ functions (Hulsmans et al., 2017) and maintenance of tissue homeostasis (Nicolás-Ávila et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies by Heidt et al., 2014 and Weinberger et al., 2020.

claim: Macrophages contribute to organ functions in healthy cardiovascular tissues.
source: They represent the most abundant immune cell population in healthy cardiovascular tissues (Heidt et al., 2014; Weinberger et al., 2020), where they contribute to organ functions (Hulsmans et al., 2017) and maintenance of tissue homeostasis (Nicolás-Ávila et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study by Hulsmans et al., 2017.

claim: Macrophages contribute to maintenance of tissue homeostasis in healthy cardiovascular tissues.
source: They represent the most abundant immune cell population in healthy cardiovascular tissues (Heidt et al., 2014; Weinberger et al., 2020), where they contribute to organ functions (Hulsmans et al., 2017) and maintenance of tissue homeostasis (Nicolás-Ávila et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study by Nicolás-Ávila et al., 2020.

claim: Acute myocardial infarction (AMI) has remained a leading cause of mortality and morbidity worldwide.
source: AMI has remained a leading cause of mortality and morbidity worldwide (Ahmad and Anderson, 2021; Lozano et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies by Ahmad and Anderson, 2021 and Lozano et al., 2012.

claim: Acute survival in myocardial infarction has improved through the broad availability of percutaneous coronary intervention.
source: Although acute survival in this condition has improved through the broad availability of percutaneous coronary intervention, adverse myocardial remodeling, and fibrosis frequently result in heart failure (Gerber et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study by Gerber et al., 2016.

claim: Adverse myocardial remodeling and fibrosis frequently result in heart failure after myocardial infarction.
source: Although acute survival in this condition has improved through the broad availability of percutaneous coronary intervention, adverse myocardial remodeling, and fibrosis frequently result in heart failure (Gerber et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study by Gerber et al., 2016.

claim: Diminished blood supply to myocardial tissue during AMI leads to acute tissue necrosis.
source: Pathophysiologically, the diminished blood supply to myocardial tissue during AMI leads to acute tissue necrosis, which induces a profound sterile inflammation and triggers complex cascade of immune processes and tissue remodeling (Hilgendorf et al., 2014; Honold and Nahrendorf, 2018; Nahrendorf et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies by Hilgendorf et al., 2014; Honold and Nahrendorf, 2018; Nahrendorf et al., 2007.

claim: Acute tissue necrosis during AMI induces a profound sterile inflammation.
source: Pathophysiologically, the diminished blood supply to myocardial tissue during AMI leads to acute tissue necrosis, which induces a profound sterile inflammation and triggers complex cascade of immune processes and tissue remodeling (Hilgendorf et al., 2014; Honold and Nahrendorf, 2018; Nahrendorf et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies by Hilgendorf et al., 2014; Honold and Nahrendorf, 2018; Nahrendorf et al., 2007.

claim: Uncontrolled immune reactions in the course of AMI are associated with impaired wound healing and adverse remodeling.
source: Consequently, uncontrolled immune reactions in the course of AMI are associated with impaired wound healing and adverse remodeling and can result in worsened cardiac outcome (Panizzi et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study by Panizzi et al., 2010.

claim: Yolk sac (YS) erythro-myeloid progenitors (EMPs) are a principal source of cardiac macrophages in adult life.
source: Fate-mapping analyses have identified yolk sac (YS) erythro-myeloid progenitors (EMPs) as a principal source of cardiac macrophages in adult life (Ginhoux et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study by Ginhoux et al., 2010.

claim: Cardiac macrophages can derive from embryonic and adult hematopoietic progenitors.
source: Cardiac macrophages can derive from embryonic and adult hematopoietic progenitors (Epelman et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study by Epelman et al., 2014.

claim: Genomic deletion of FIRE in the Csf1r gene leads to a selective absence of tissue macrophages without the developmental defects observed in Csf1r−/− mice.
source: In Csf1r∆FIRE mice, genetic deletion of the FIRE in the first intron of the Csf1r gene leads to a selective absence of tissue macrophages without the developmental defects observed in Csf1r−/− mice (Munro et al., 2020; Rojo et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies by Munro et al., 2020 and Rojo et al., 2019.

claim: DT-mediated cell ablation is known to induce neutrophil recruitment and tissue inflammation.
source: However, DT-mediated cell ablation is known to induce neutrophil recruitment and tissue inflammation (Frieler et al., 2015; Oh et al., 2017; Ruedl and Jung, 2018; Sivakumaran et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies by Frieler et al., 2015; Oh et al., 2017; Ruedl and Jung, 2018; Sivakumaran et al., 2016.

claim: Inflammatory preconditioning of cardiac tissue after DT-depletion is likely to impact on cardiac remodeling and influence assessment of tissue macrophage functions.
source: This inflammatory preconditioning of cardiac tissue after DT-depletion is likely to impact on cardiac remodeling and influence assessment of tissue macrophage functions.
evidence: Inferred from known effects of DT-mediated depletion on tissue inflammation, cited from Frieler et al., 2015; Oh et al., 2017; Ruedl and Jung, 2018; Sivakumaran et al., 2016.

claim: Inflammatory polarization of neutrophils has been associated with poor outcome after ischemic brain injury.
source: Interestingly, inflammatory polarization of neutrophils have also been associated with poor outcome after ischemic brain injury (Cuartero et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study by Cuartero et al., 2013.

claim: Clinical trials in myocardial infarction patients show a correlation of inflammatory markers with extent of myocardial damage.
source: Clinical trials in myocardial infarction patients show a correlation of inflammatory markers with extent of the myocardial damage (Sánchez et al., 2006) and with short- and long-term mortality (Mueller et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study by Sánchez et al., 2006.

claim: Clinical trials in myocardial infarction patients show a correlation of inflammatory markers with short- and long-term mortality.
source: Clinical trials in myocardial infarction patients show a correlation of inflammatory markers with extent of the myocardial damage (Sánchez et al., 2006) and with short- and long-term mortality (Mueller et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study by Mueller et al., 2002.

claim: Depletion of macrophages by anti-CSF1R treatment is associated with worsened cardiac function in a model of pressure overload induced heart failure.
source: In line with our findings, depletion of macrophages by anti-CSF1R treatment was associated with worsened cardiac function in a model of pressure overload induced heart failure (Revelo et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study by Revelo et al., 2021.

claim: Depletion of recruited macrophages only in the initial phase of myocardial infarction improved cardiac healing in Ccr2DTR mice.
source: Controversially, a recent study in which monocytes were depleted using DT-injections in Ccr2DTR mice reported beneficial effects on cardiac outcome after MI in mice (Bajpai et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study by Bajpai et al., 2019.

claim: Ccr2-deficient mice exhibit reduced acute recruitment of neutrophils to the brain after I/R injury.
source: In line with this, Ccr2-deficient mice exhibit reduced acute recruitment of neutrophils to the brain after I/R injury, which was associated with reduced infarct size and brain edema (Dimitrijevic et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study by Dimitrijevic et al., 2007.

claim: Reduced neutrophil recruitment in Ccr2-deficient mice after brain I/R injury is associated with reduced infarct size and brain edema.
source: In line with this, Ccr2-deficient mice exhibit reduced acute recruitment of neutrophils to the brain after I/R injury, which was associated with reduced infarct size and brain edema (Dimitrijevic et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study by Dimitrijevic et al., 2007.
